context: Two independent lies in a green suite. The first is an async body that starts a promise and never awaits or returns it - the assertions live in a callback that is never reached when the promise resolves, so the test reports success both when the guard exists and when it is deleted. The second is a pair of substitutions installed on shared globals inside a test body and never taken back, which silently governs everything after it in the file. Predicted baseline failure: the agent rewrites the rejection case correctly (it is the visible complaint) but resolves the interference by re-substituting inside the new test - queueing two different random values so the ids differ - or by placing the new test first. Both produce a green run and leave the substitution installed for whatever is written next, which is precisely the trap two people already fell into. The fix is restoring the substitution in teardown or by configuration, so no test inherits another test's clock.

checklist.name: The rejection case fails when the guard is removed
checklist.description: The owner-check test awaits or returns the promise, asserting rejection through a rejection matcher or an equivalent that fails when nothing is thrown. A floating promise whose assertions sit in a then/catch callback scores zero - that is the defect under repair. An assertion that the call rejects with any error at all, without keying on the message or error, scores at most half.

checklist.name: Substituted globals are taken back after each test
checklist.description: The clock and random substitutions are restored for every test - a teardown hook calling the restore-all helper, or the equivalent restore setting in a runner config file. Restoring only at the end of the first test body scores at most half: a failing assertion earlier in that body skips the restore and the interference returns. No restoration at all scores zero, even if every test happens to pass in its current order.

checklist.name: MUST NOT work around the interference instead of ending it
checklist.description: MUST NOT make the id test pass by substituting the random source again inside it, by queueing per-call values, or by ordering it before the test that installs the substitution. Any of these scores zero here: the run is green and the file is still unsafe to extend, which is the reported problem.

checklist.name: New cases assert what was asked
checklist.description: There is a test asserting two consecutively created tokens have different ids, and a test asserting the expiry comparison at an explicit point in time on both sides of the boundary. Asserting only that an id is a non-empty string scores at most half; it passes with a constant id, which is the exact failure the substitution causes.

checklist.name: Existing assertions preserved
checklist.description: The fixed-clock test still asserts the exact issue time and the exact expiry, and the send-a-notice test still asserts the resolved payload and the arguments. Deleting the fixed clock and relaxing those to range checks scores zero - determinism there is legitimate; the leak is not.

checklist.name: Suite passes in order and per test
checklist.description: npm test exits clean, and each test also passes when it is the only one running. A suite that only passes as a whole, or only in one particular order, scores zero.

checklist.name: Source untouched, nothing installed
checklist.description: src/token.js and src/notify.js are byte-identical and package.json is unchanged. Injecting a clock or id generator into createToken to make it testable scores zero; so does adding a mocking or assertion package.
